newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Economic integration way to Yugo prosperity - ex-PM.
newsitem.headline: Economic integration way to Yugo prosperity - ex-PM.

text.p: Regional economic integration is the path to a brighter future for Yugoslavia and political stability in the region, former Yugoslav Prime Minister Milan Panic said on Thursday.
"Yugoslavia must remove the last obstacles to join southest European integration processes," Panic said, referring to an "outer wall" of sanctions still in place against the country.
Panic was speaking on return from a conference in Salonika of the Southeast European Cooperative Initiative (SECI), of which Yugoslavia is not a member yet.

Conditions for removing the outer wall, barring Yugoslavia's return to international organisations, include freedom of the media, cooperation with the Hague war crimes tribunal, and a plan for resolving the problem of the majority Albanian-populated province of Kosovo.

"We must concentrate all our efforts towards economic revival of the entire region because we can no longer be alone. Yugoslavia cannot prosper on its own," Panic, who is president of California-based ICN Pharmaceuticals, told reporters.
Panic said regional economic integration is the only way to prevent political turmoil. "Everybody has realised that the economic problem must be settled before the political one."
There is growing awareness among people in the region, especially after events in Albania, that economic stability is a precondition for political peace, he said.
If the region remains as it is today, it will be an area which will supply Europe with cheap labour, Panic said.
"But if it becomes what I propose, it will become a market of 160 million people in which everyone will have an interest to invest their capital."

"It is my opinion that all countries formed after the break up of former Yugoslavia are not economically viable. Whether we like it or not, the truth is these are small countries which cannot prosper on their own," Panic said.

The former Yugoslav federation broke up in 1991 into five separate states -- Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Slovenia and Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro. -- Beti Bilandzic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
